title: Leg weakness with an epidural: suspected epidural haematoma

header.contentArea: Perioperative care: complications of epidural analgesia and neuraxial anticoagulation
guidelineVersions: FPM Best practice in the management of epidural analgesia in the hospital setting (third edition, 2025)
Association of Anaesthetists, OAA and RA-UK: Regional anaesthesia and patients with abnormalities of coagulation (Anaesthesia, 2013)

related.why: Cauda equina syndrome: the same time-critical compression logic
Anatomy of the lumbar spine and vertebral canal

brief.scenario: Mrs Angela Oldroyd, 68, is on day 1 after an emergency laparotomy. A thoracic epidural infusion was started before surgery. She is on prophylactic enoxaparin. The nurse reports that she can no longer lift her legs and they feel numb.
brief.task: Discuss your assessment and management with the examiner.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: A thoracic epidural should not paralyse the legs. New or worsening leg weakness is compression until MRI says otherwise.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Calling it 'the epidural working' and rechecking at the next ward round.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd see her now: stop the infusion, check sensory level and Bromage score, and call the anaesthetist."

grid.label: Assess the block formally
grid.fail: Accepts numb, weak legs as the expected epidural effect without examining her.
grid.pass: Checks sensory level to cold, Bromage score, back pain and tenderness, temperature, observations and the drug chart.
grid.high: Knows a thoracic epidural should spare leg power, so a dense leg motor block is abnormal from the start.

grid.label: Differential diagnosis
grid.pass: Excess local anaesthetic or catheter migration, epidural haematoma, epidural abscess, and cord ischaemia or nerve injury.
grid.high: Back pain, anticoagulation or recent catheter handling point to haematoma; fever and local tenderness point to abscess.

grid.label: Stop, reassess and escalate (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Leaves the infusion running and observes until the next ward round.
grid.pass: Stops the infusion, calls the anaesthetist now, reassesses hourly; escalates if no improvement over two consecutive hours or any worsening.
grid.high: Does not wait if the block is worsening or there is new back pain: MRI now.

grid.label: Urgent MRI and neurosurgery
grid.fail: Requests a routine MRI, or waits for the morning team.
grid.pass: Urgent MRI spine and urgent neurosurgical discussion; withholds enoxaparin; checks platelets and clotting.
grid.high: Runs these in parallel, because recovery depends on early decompression; keeps her nil by mouth for possible surgery.

grid.label: LMWH timing around the epidural
grid.fail: Quotes one flat interval for every step, or gives LMWH regardless of the catheter.
grid.pass: Prophylactic LMWH: 12 hours before insertion or catheter removal; next dose at least 4 hours after insertion or removal.
grid.high: Treatment-dose LMWH needs 24 hours; knows catheter removal is the highest-risk moment, so it is timed like insertion.

grid.label: Explain and document
grid.fail: Tells her it is normal and does not document.
grid.pass: Explains honestly, informs the registrar and consultant, and documents findings and actions.
grid.high: Records exact times of onset, each assessment and each call, and updates her family with her consent.

grid.label: Other epidural complications
grid.pass: Hypotension, urinary retention, pruritus, respiratory depression, dural puncture headache and local anaesthetic toxicity.
grid.high: Dural puncture headache is postural; an epidural blood patch is offered if conservative treatment fails.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The nurse says her legs are numb and weak. What do you do?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That's the epidural working. I'd ask the nurse to keep an eye on it until the ward round.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: When can she have her enoxaparin?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: You leave four hours either side of anything to do with the epidural.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd reassure her it's normal. I don't think it needs writing up.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I can't think of any others.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The nurse says her legs are numb and weak. What do you do?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd see her now: sensory level to cold, Bromage score, any back pain or tenderness, temperature, observations and the drug chart.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Too much local anaesthetic or a migrated catheter, an epidural haematoma, an abscess, or cord ischaemia or nerve injury.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Stop the infusion, call the anaesthetist, and reassess hourly. If there's no improvement over two hours or it gets worse, it's escalated.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: An hour later her legs are weaker.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Urgent MRI spine and urgent discussion with neurosurgery. I'd withhold her enoxaparin and check platelets and clotting.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: When is enoxaparin safe around an epidural?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: For a prophylactic dose, 12 hours before insertion or catheter removal, and the next dose at least 4 hours after either.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: My registrar and consultant. I'd explain to Mrs Oldroyd honestly and document everything.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hypotension, urinary retention, itching, respiratory depression, post-dural puncture headache and local anaesthetic toxicity.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The nurse says her legs are numb and weak.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This is a thoracic epidural, so her legs should have normal power. A dense leg block is abnormal before I even examine her.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She has new pain between her shoulder blades.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: With enoxaparin on board, back pain and progressive weakness point to a haematoma. If she were febrile with local tenderness, I'd think abscess.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Would you wait two hours after stopping it?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Not with worsening weakness and back pain. I'd stop the infusion and request the MRI now, not after two hours.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: MRI can't scan her for three hours.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd escalate through my consultant and the anaesthetist, and talk to neurosurgery in parallel, because the chance of recovery falls the longer the cord is compressed. She stays nil by mouth.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The nurse asks whether to pull the catheter.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Not yet. Removal is the highest-risk moment for bleeding, so it follows the same timing as insertion: 12 hours after a prophylactic dose, 24 after a treatment dose, and the anaesthetist decides.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: With exact times: when the weakness started, each assessment, and each call. I'd update her husband with her permission.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She asks about the headache she had yesterday.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If it's postural it may be a dural puncture headache. Fluids, analgesia and caffeine first; a blood patch if that fails.

failures.move: Treating new leg weakness as the epidural working and leaving the infusion running.
failures.consequence: A compressing haematoma goes unrecognised until paraplegia is permanent.

failures.move: Requesting a routine MRI and waiting for the day team.
failures.consequence: Delay to decompression reduces the chance of neurological recovery.
Haematoma and abscess, both surgical emergencies, are missed.

failures.move: Giving or omitting LMWH without regard to catheter insertion and removal times.
failures.consequence: Raises the risk of epidural haematoma, or leaves her unprotected against VTE.

recovery.when: You called it the expected block
recovery.line: A thoracic epidural shouldn't weaken the legs, so I'd stop the infusion and get the anaesthetist to see her now.
There are two: 12 hours after a prophylactic dose before insertion or removal, then at least 4 hours before the next dose.

knowledge.fact: Escalate if a dense motor block does not improve over two consecutive hours after stopping the infusion, or worsens hour to hour.
Suspected haematoma or abscess: urgent MRI and urgent neurosurgical discussion.
Prophylactic LMWH: 12 hours before insertion or catheter removal; next dose 4 hours after either. Treatment dose: 24 hours before.
NAP3 identified catheter removal as the time of greatest risk for epidural haematoma.
Post-dural puncture headache is postural; a blood patch is offered if conservative treatment fails.

recall.think: Epidural haematoma or abscess compressing the cord.
recall.say: "New leg weakness with an epidural: compression until MRI excludes it."
do: Stop the infusion; sensory level and Bromage

numbers.meaning: after prophylactic LMWH before insertion or removal
after insertion or removal before next LMWH

recall.finish: Urgent MRI and decompression if a haematoma is found.

sources.name: Faculty of Pain Medicine of the Royal College of Anaesthetists. Best practice in the management of epidural analgesia in the hospital setting
sources.supports: Monitor sensory and motor block with the Bromage score (7.13); escalate if dense motor block does not improve for two consecutive hours after stopping the infusion, or worsens from one hour to the next (7.15); suspected vertebral canal haematoma or abscess: urgent MRI and urgent discussion with the neurosurgical unit; NAP3 found catheter removal to be the time of greatest risk for epidural haematoma

sources.supports: Table 1: prophylactic LMWH 12 hours before neuraxial block, next dose 4 hours after block or catheter removal; treatment-dose LMWH 24 hours before block, next dose 4 hours after (24 hours if the block was traumatic); catheter removal follows the same timings as insertion

partner.opening: Mrs Oldroyd had a thoracic epidural sited before her laparotomy yesterday. The nurse says she can't lift her legs and they feel numb. What would you do?
partner.actorBrief: You are the examiner. Release findings only when the candidate asks or examines. Push on the LMWH timings if the candidate gives a single interval.

reveals.finding: Reduced sensation to cold from T10 downwards on both sides. Cannot lift either leg against gravity; can move the toes. Yesterday evening she could lift both legs.

reveals.trigger: Asks about back pain, fever or the site
reveals.finding: New aching pain in the mid-back since 06:00. T 36.9°C. Catheter site clean, no tenderness.
Epidural sited 08:30 yesterday. Enoxaparin 40 mg SC at 18:00 yesterday. No antiplatelets. Platelets 210.

reveals.trigger: Reassesses one hour after stopping the infusion
reveals.finding: Weakness is worse: she can no longer move her toes.

push.question: How would you assess her?
push.expect: Sensory level to cold, Bromage score, back pain, fever, observations, drug chart.

push.question: What is the differential?
push.expect: LA excess or catheter migration, haematoma, abscess, cord ischaemia or nerve injury.

push.question: What do you do first?
push.expect: Stop infusion, anaesthetist now, hourly reassessment; escalate if no improvement or worsening.

push.question: Her weakness is worse. Now what?
push.expect: Urgent MRI spine and neurosurgery in parallel; withhold LMWH; clotting and platelets.

push.question: When can LMWH be given around an epidural?
push.expect: Prophylactic: 12 h before insertion or removal; next dose 4 h after; treatment dose 24 h.

push.question: Name other complications of epidurals.
push.expect: Hypotension, retention, pruritus, respiratory depression, PDPH, LA toxicity.

curveballs.prompt: The registrar says to wait for the morning ward round.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Escalate to the consultant and anaesthetist now; progressive weakness is time-critical.

curveballs.prompt: Her 18:00 enoxaparin is due. Should the nurse give it?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: withhold until the haematoma is excluded and the anaesthetist has advised on catheter removal.

curveballs.prompt: She is febrile with a red, tender catheter site instead.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Suspect epidural abscess: urgent MRI, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, neurosurgical discussion.
Honest: it is serious, it is being treated as an emergency, and outcome is better the sooner it is treated.
